translations.text: After Joshua son of Nun died, the people of Israel asked the Lord, saying, “Who will go ahead of us against the Canaanites to fight them?”
The Lord said to them, “Judah is the one who will go ahead of you. Look, I have handed the land over to him.”
Judah said to his brother Simeon, “Come up with me into my allotted territory, and let us fight the Canaanites. I will also go with you into your allotted territory.” So Simeon went with him.
Judah went up with him, and the Lord of Israel handed the Canaanites and the Perizzites over to them. They killed ten thousand of them at Bezek.
They found Adoni-bezek and fought at Bezek. They killed the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
Adoni-bezek fled. He pursued him, and they caught him and cut off his thumbs and his big toes.

Adoni-bezek said, “Seventy kings, with their thumbs and big toes cut off, used to gather what was under my table. Just as I did to them, so God has repaid me.” They brought him up to Jerusalem, and he died there.
The people of Judah fought against Jerusalem. They fought against it, captured it, struck it with the edge of the sword, and burned the city with fire.
After this, the people of Judah went down to fight the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, the south, and the lowlands, that is, the land in the valley.

Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron, and Hebron came out to fight him. Hebron had formerly been called Kiriath-arba-sepher. They defeated Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, descendants of Anak.
They moved from there against those who lived in Debir. Debir had formerly been called Kiriath-sepher, which is the city of writings.
Caleb said, “Whoever attacks the city of writings and captures it, I will give him my daughter Achsah as his wife.”
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured the city, and Caleb gave him his daughter as his wife.

As she was coming out, he urged her to ask her father for a field. She grumbled and cried out while riding the beast of burden, “You have given me land in the south!” Caleb said to her, “What is wrong? What do you want?”

Achsah said to him, “Give me a blessing. Since you have given me land in the south, give me a spring of water.” Caleb gave her what she wanted: a spring in the heights and a spring in the lowlands, the mountain and what belonged to it, and what was on the eastern side.

The son of Hobab the Kenite, Moses’ father-in-law, went up to the City of Palms with the people of Judah, out into the wilderness south of Judah, on the road leading down to Arad. They went and settled with the people of Amalek.
Judah went with his brother Simeon. They killed the Canaanites who lived in Zephath, destroyed it, and devoted it to destruction. They called the city Anathema.
Judah struck Gaza and all its territory, but neither Ekron nor its territory, nor Ashdod nor its territory.
The Lord was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country. They could not take possession of the inhabitants of the plain, because Rechab came out, and they had iron chariots.
Caleb gave him Hebron, about which Moses had spoken to them. From there he took possession of the three cities of the descendants of Anak, and they removed the three sons of Anak from there.
The people of Benjamin did not dispossess the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem. The Jebusites lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.
The descendants of Joseph went up to Bethel, and the Lord was with them.
They took hold of Bethel. The city’s former name was Luz.
The watchmen looked and saw a man who had come out of the city. They seized him and said, “Show us the way into the city, and we will show you mercy.”
He showed them the way into the city. They struck the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and his family go.
The man went up to the land of the Hittites and built a city there. He named it Luz, and that is its name to this day.

And Manasseh did not drive out the people of Beth-shan, which is the city of the Scythians, or its villages or those around it, or those living in Aikthaena or those around it or its villages, or those living in Balak or those around it or its villages, or those living in Megiddo or those around it or its villages, or those living in Ibleam or those around it or its villages. And the Canaanites began to settle in this land.
Then, when Israel became strong, it made the Canaanites pay tribute to it, but did not drive them out completely.
And Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer. Instead, the Canaanites lived among them in Gezer and paid tribute.
And Zebulun did not drive out those living in Kedron or those living in Maad. The Canaanites lived among them and paid tribute to them.

And Asher did not drive out those living in Sacho, but paid tribute to them, nor those living in Dor, nor those living in Sidon, nor those living in Dalab and Achzib, and Hebron and Achzib, and Hebron and Aphek
and Rehob. And Asher lived among the Canaanites who lived in the land, because it could not muster the strength to drive them out.

And they paid tribute to it. And Naphtali did not drive out those living in Beth-shemesh or those living in Beth-anath. And Israel lived among the Canaanites who lived in the land. But those living in Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath paid tribute to them.
And the Amorites forced the descendants of Dan up into the mountains, because they did not allow them to come down into the plain.

And the Amorites stubbornly insisted on coming down to live on the stony mountain, in the rugged place where the bears and foxes were, and in the myrtle grove, or on the mountain of myrtles, in Sem. And the power of the house of Joseph grew strong over the Amorites, and they paid tribute to them.
The hill country of the Amorites extended from the ascent of Akrabbim, from the rock upward.

And the angel of the Lord went up to Gilgal, up to the place of weeping, and up to Bethel. He spoke to the Israelites, saying to them, “This is what the Lord says: I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to your ancestors I would give you. And I told you, ‘I will not remove your descendants. I will never break my covenant with you.’

“You must not make a covenant with those who live in this land, nor worship their gods. Instead, you must smash their carved images and tear down their altars. But you have not obeyed my voice. Why have you done these things?”

“I, for my part, will no longer continue removing the people whom I said I would cast out. So I will not drive them out before you. Instead, they will bring you distress and further deception, and their other gods will become a stumbling block to you.”
When the angel of the Lord spoke these words to the Israelites, the people cried out and wept.
For this reason they named that place Klauthmon, which means “the place of weeping.” And they offered a sacrifice to the Lord there.
And Joshua sent the people away, and the Israelites went, each to his own inheritance, to take possession of his land.

And the people served the Lord throughout Joshua’s lifetime and throughout the lifetime of the elders who had spent a long time with Joshua, who knew the great work that the Lord had done among Israel.
And Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of 110.
And they buried him within the territory of his inheritance, in Timnath-heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
And that entire generation died and was gathered to their ancestors. Another generation arose after them, who did not know the Lord or the work he had done among Israel.
And the Israelites did evil in the sight of the Lord and served the Baals.

They abandoned the Lord, the God of their ancestors, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went and followed other gods from among the gods of the nations around them. They worshiped them and provoked the Lord to anger.
They abandoned him and served Baal and Astarte.

And the Lord became angry with the Israelites. He handed them over to plunderers, who plundered them, and he handed them over to their enemies around them. They could no longer stand against their enemies.
In everything they undertook, the Lord's hand was against them, bringing harm upon them, just as the Lord had said and just as the Lord had sworn to them. He afflicted them severely.
And the Lord raised up judges over them, and the Lord rescued them from the hands of those who plundered them.

But they did not listen to their judges either, because they went and prostituted themselves by following other gods and worshiped them. They angered the Lord and quickly turned away from the path their ancestors had followed in obeying the Lord's words. They did not do as their ancestors had done.

And the Lord raised up judges over them, and the Lord was with the judge. He rescued them from the hands of their enemies throughout the judge's lifetime, because they pleaded with the Lord through their groaning before those who fought against them and oppressed them.

And whenever the judge died, they turned back again and became more corrupt than their ancestors, going after other gods to serve and worship them. They did not abandon their stubborn ways or their other deeds.
And the Lord became angry with Israel and said, “Because this nation has abandoned my covenant, which I commanded their ancestors to keep, and has not obeyed my voice,
I too will no longer remove before them a single person from the nations that Joshua son of Nun left behind, and which he left behind
to test Israel through them, to see whether they would keep to the Lord's path and walk in it as their ancestors had kept to it, or not.”
And the Lord left these nations behind rather than removing them immediately, and he did not hand them over to Joshua.
And these are the nations that the Lord left behind to test Israel through them—all those who had not experienced warfare in Canaan—
so that the generations of the Israelites would learn, by being taught warfare, which they had not known, unlike those before them:
the five territories of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in Lebanon, from Mount Baal-Hermon to Lebo-Hamath.
And they were left behind to test Israel through them, to find out whether they would obey the Lord's commandments, which he had commanded their ancestors through Moses.
And the Israelites lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
And they took their daughters as wives for themselves, and gave their own daughters to their sons as wives. They served their gods.
And the Israelites did evil in the Lord's sight. They forgot the Lord their God and served the Baals and the sacred groves.
The Lord blazed with anger against Israel and handed them over to Cushan-Rishathaim, king of Syria in Mesopotamia. The people of Israel served Cushan-Rishathaim for eight years.
And the Israelites cried out to the Lord. He raised up a deliverer for Israel, who rescued them: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.

And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel. When he went out to war to fight Cushan-rishathaim, the Lord handed Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, over to him, and he prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim.
And the land had peace for fifty years. Then Othniel son of Kenaz died.
The Israelites again did evil in the Lord's sight, and the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against Israel because they had done evil in the Lord's sight.
He gathered to himself all the people of Ammon and Amalek. He went and struck down the people of Israel and took possession of the City of Palms.
And the Israelites served Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years.

The Israelites cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up a deliverer for them to save them: Ehud son of Gera, son of Benjamin, a man who could use both hands equally well. The Israelites sent gifts through him to Eglon king of Moab.
Ehud made himself a sword sharpened on both sides, a span long. He fastened it to his belt on his right side, under his embroidered robe.
He presented the gifts to Eglon king of Moab. Eglon was a very handsome man.
When Ehud had finished giving him the gifts, he sent away the men who had brought the gifts with him.
Eglon turned back from the idols at Gilgal. Ehud said to the king, “I have a secret message from God to tell you, O king.” Eglon said to him, “Be quiet!” He sent away those standing before him.
Ehud went in to him. The king was sitting alone in his cool upstairs room. Ehud said to him, “I have a message from God to tell you, O king.” Eglon rose from his throne and approached him.
As he was rising, Ehud stretched out his left hand, took the sword fastened to his right thigh, and plunged it into Eglon.
He also sank the hilt into him, into his belly, so that the belly covered the sword, because he did not pull the sword out of him.
Ehud came out from the place where he was and went out past the guards, having shut and secured the doors of his upper room.

When he came out, he was [?] and walked away. The king’s servants went in and saw that the doors of his upstairs room were locked. They said to one another, “Perhaps he is relieving himself in the cool room.”
They waited until they were embarrassed, but no one opened the upstairs doors. They took the key and opened them, and there was their lord lying dead on the ground.
Ehud escaped during the confusion they had fallen into. He passed by them all without anyone suspecting him, until he reached Seirah safely.
When he arrived, he blew the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites came down with him from the hills, and he walked ahead of them.

He said to them, “Follow me, because the Lord God has handed over our enemies, Moab, to you.” They followed him and took control of the crossing places of the Jordan in the land of Moab. They did not allow anyone to cross there.
At that time they struck down about ten thousand men of Moab, all its fighting men and every powerful man. No one escaped them.
The land of Moab was humbled that day under Israel’s hand, and the land had peace for eighty years. Ehud judged them until he died.
After him, Shamgar son of Anath arose. He struck down about six hundred Philistine men with a plowshare used for oxen. He too saved the Israelites, and Shamgar died.
The people of Israel again did evil in the Lord’s sight.
The Lord handed them over to Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was named Sisera, and he lived in Harosheth of the nations.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord because he had nine hundred iron chariots, and he had severely oppressed the Israelites for twenty years.
Deborah, a woman who was a prophet and the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time.
Deborah sat under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites came up to her to receive judgment from her.

Deborah sent for Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in the hill country of Naphtali. She said to him, “Has not the Lord, the God of Israel, commanded you? Go up to Mount Tabor and take with you ten thousand men from the people of Naphtali and from the people of Zebulun.”
And I will come to you down at the Kishon stream, against Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, and against his chariots, his horses, and his troops. And the Lord will hand him over to you.
Barak said to her, “If you come with me, I will go. But if you do not come, I will not go, because I do not know the day on which the Lord's angel will go out with me.”

Deborah said to him, “I will certainly go with you. But know that you will not have the leading honor on the journey you are going to make. Instead, the Lord will hand Sisera over to a woman.” Deborah got up and went with Barak from Kedesh in Naphtali.
Barak summoned Zebulun and Naphtali from Kedesh. Ten thousand men came up on foot, and Deborah went up with him to Mount Tabor.
Heber the Kenite had separated himself from the descendants of Jobab, Moses' father-in-law. He pitched his tent by the tree at the resting place near Kedesh.
They told Sisera that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor.
Sisera summoned all his chariots—nine hundred iron chariots—and all the troops with him, from Harosheth of the nations down to the Kishon stream.
Deborah said to Barak, “Get up! This is the day on which the Lord has handed Sisera over to you. Look, the Lord will go ahead of you!” And Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men.
The Lord threw Sisera, all his chariots, and his entire army into confusion before Barak at the edge of the sword. Sisera jumped down from his chariot and fled on foot.
Barak pursued his chariots and his army as far as Harosheth, the wooded place of the nations. Sisera's entire army fell by the edge of the sword; not a single one of them remained.
But Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the household of Heber the Kenite.
Jael went out to meet Sisera and said to him, “Come in here, my lord! Come in here! Do not be afraid.” He went into her tent, and she covered him with a haircloth blanket.
Sisera said to her, “Give me a little water to drink, because I am thirsty.” She opened the skin of milk, gave him a drink, and covered him.
He said to her, “Stand at the entrance to the tent. If someone comes to you and asks, ‘Is anyone here?’ tell him, ‘No.’” And she covered him with her hide covering.

Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, took a tent peg and held a hammer in her hand. She went quietly up to him and drove the peg into his temple. He fell to the ground, collapsed at her feet, breathed his last, and died.

Then Barak came, pursuing Sisera. Jael went out to meet him and said to him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are looking for.” He went in with her, and there was Sisera, lying dead on the ground, with the peg driven into his temple.
On that day the Lord God humbled Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites.
The power of the Israelites continued to grow stronger against Jabin king of Canaan until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang a song, saying:
“When the leaders of Israel took the lead, with the people's willingness, because a revelation was revealed in Israel, when the people acted of their own free will, bless the Lord!
Listen, kings! Pay attention, powerful governors! I belong to the Lord; I belong to him. I will sing and make music to the Lord, the God of Israel.
Lord, when you came out from Seir, when you came out from the countryside of Edom, the earth shook, the sky stood still, and the clouds poured down water.
The mountains shook before the Lord at Sinai, before the Lord, the God of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the kings failed. They abandoned the highways and traveled along winding, crooked paths.
The living failed; the mighty in Israel failed. They failed until Deborah awoke, until a mother arose in Israel.
They chose new gods for themselves. Then they fought against the cities of the rulers. Was a shield ever seen, or a small shield or a spear, among the forty thousand in Israel?
My heart is stirred toward the leaders of Israel’s territory, the rulers of the people, those who willingly serve among the people. Bless the Lord!
You who ride female donkeys and sit in wagons, and who sit at the place of judgment at noon, and who walk on wooded roads, speak along the way.

At the sound of those making music among those rejoicing, they will give justice there to the Lord. Increase, you righteous people, and grow strong in Israel! Then the Lord’s people went up to his cities.
Arise, arise, Deborah! Arise, arise, you who sing a song with strength! Rise up, Barak, and lead your captives away, son of Abinoam! And Deborah strengthened Barak and increased his strength.
Then the strong will come down, a remnant of the mighty among the people, and the Lord will come down to him among the strong.
The people of Ephraim punished them among the [?], their brother Benjamin. Machir is with me as a leader. They came down, advancing, and those from Zebulun drew with a scribe’s rod of instruction.

The leaders of Issachar were with Deborah, and Barak was with Issachar. This is how Barak sent them into the valleys through his messengers. From the divisions of Reuben came the great searchers of the heart.
Why did they sit in the middle of the road called Digomia [?], to listen to the sound of the messengers? At Reuben’s division, great men searched their hearts.
Gilead remained on the bank of the Jordan, in the place where he had settled. And Dan—why does he linger by the ships? Asher sat on the seacoast.
And Zebulun settled along his routes leading out, a people who exposed their lives to death, and Naphtali on the heights of the field.
Their kings came and spread out to fight. Then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo. They received no gift of silver.
The stars from heaven stood in their courses to fight against Sisera.
The torrent of Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent of Kishon. My soul, which is strong, will trample them.
Then the horse’s hooves broke in the turmoil, and my hoof will stamp down on them. Where will his mighty men flee?
“Curse the place called Meroz,” said the angel of the Lord. “Curse it! Its inhabitants are cursed because they did not come to help. The Lord is there to help among the mighty.”
May Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, be blessed among women. May she be blessed by the women in the tents.
He asked for water; she gave him milk. In a bowl fit for the mighty, she brought him butter.

She stretched out her left hand to the tent peg, and she stretched out her right hand to the workers’ hammer. She drove it into Sisera’s temple. She crushed his head, struck him, and crushed his temple.
He fell at her feet, rolled over, and collapsed. He lay between her feet. He threw himself down and remained as he had fallen. There he fell, cast down.
Sisera’s mother looked out through the window, the opening in the lattice, because his chariots hesitated to come and the wheels of his chariots were late in coming.
The wise women who understood her answered her, and she herself repeated her words to herself.

“Will they not find him dividing spoils? The compassionate man will have compassion on the head of a man. Dyed spoils for Sisera, dyed spoils, colored embroidery for the necks of those who embroider, spoils wrapped around his neck.”
May all your enemies perish like this, Lord! And may those who love him be like the sunrise coming out in its strength. And the land was at rest for forty years.
After these things, the people of Israel did evil in the Lord’s sight, and the Lord handed them over to Midian for seven years.
And Midian’s hand grew heavy upon Israel. Because of Midian, the Israelites made themselves dens in the mountains, caves, and houses of rock.
Whenever the Israelites sowed their fields, Midian would come up with Amalek and the people from the east. They would come with Midian and descend upon them.
They would destroy the produce of the land until they reached Gaza, leaving no means of staying alive in the land of Israel, nor a cow nor a donkey among their livestock.

For they and their livestock would come up with their tents. They came like swarms of locusts, and they and their camels were beyond counting. They would come up into the land of Israel and destroy it.
And Israel became very poor because of Midian.
And the Israelites cried out to the Lord because of Midian.

And the Lord sent a man, a prophet, to the Israelites. He said to them, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: I am the one who brought you up out of the land of Egypt and brought you out of the house of your slavery.
And I rescued you from the power of Egypt and from the power of all those who oppressed you. I drove them out before you and gave you their land.
And I told you, ‘I am the Lord your God. Do not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you are living.’ But you did not obey my voice.”

Now an angel of the Lord came down and sat beneath the terebinth of Ephraim, which is in Shechem, on the land of Joash, the father of Esdri. Gideon, his son, was threshing wheat in a winepress to keep it away from Midian.
And the angel of the Lord appeared to him and said to him, “The Lord, mighty in power, is with you.”

And Gideon said to him, “Listen to me, lord. If the Lord is with us, why have all these troubles come upon us? And where are all his wonders that our ancestors told us about, saying, ‘Did not the Lord bring us up out of Egypt?’ But now the Lord has cast us away from him and handed us over to Midian.”
And the angel of the Lord looked at him and said to him, “Go in this strength of yours, and you will rescue Israel from the power of Midian. Look, I have sent you to go.”
Gideon said to him, “Listen to me, my lord. How will I save Israel? Look, my group of a thousand men is weak in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s household.”
The angel of the Lord said to him, “The Lord will be with you, and you will strike down Midian as though it were one man.”
Gideon said to him, “If I have found favor with you, and you will do for me everything you have told me today…”
“Do not leave this place until I come to you and bring out my offering and set it before you.” The angel said to him, “Look, I will stay until you come.”

And Gideon went up to his house and prepared a young goat. He also made a measure of flour into unleavened bread. He put the meat in a basket and poured the broth into the pot. He brought them out to him beneath the terebinth and set them before him.
The angel of God said to him, “Take the meat and the unleavened bread and set them down beside that rock, and pour out the broth.” Gideon did these things.

And the angel of the Lord stretched out the end of the staff in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread. Fire came out of the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread. And the angel of the Lord went up before his eyes.
And Gideon realized that this was an angel of the Lord. Gideon said, “Woe to me, Lord God, because I have seen the angel of the Lord face to face!”
The Lord said to him, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid. You will not die.”
And Gideon built an altar to the Lord in that place and called it “The Peace of the Lord.” To this day it is still in Ephrathah, the land of the father of Esdri.
That night the Lord said to him, “Take your father’s young bull and another bull seven years old. Tear down the altar of Baal that belongs to your father, and cut down the grove above it.

Build an altar to the Lord your God, who appeared to you, on the summit of this Mount Maoch, which is at the place of battle. Take the bull and offer it as a burnt offering on the wood of the grove that you will cut down.”

Gideon took ten men from among his servants and did as the Lord had told him. But because he was afraid of his father's household and the men of the city, he did not do this during the day; he did it at night.

The men of the city rose early in the morning, and there was Baal's altar, torn down, and the grove above it had been destroyed. They saw the strong bull that he had offered as a burnt offering on the altar he had built.
The men said to one another, “Who did this?” They asked and investigated, and they learned that Gideon son of Joash had done this.
The men of the city said to Joash, “Bring your son out so that he may die, because he tore down Baal's altar and cut down the grove above it.”

Joash said to all the men who had risen against him, “Are you now going to plead Baal's case? Or are you going to save him? Whoever pleads his case must die by morning. If he is a god, let him bring a case against him, because his altar has been torn down.”
That day he named him Jerubbaal, saying, “Let Baal bring a case against him, because his altar has been torn down.”
All Midian, Amalek, and the people of the east gathered together. They marched and came down into the valley of Israel.
And the Spirit of the Lord strengthened Gideon. He blew a horn trumpet and called Abiezer to come and follow him.

He sent messengers into the land of Manasseh and summoned the other one to follow him. He also sent messengers into the land of Asher and into the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, and they came up to meet him.
Gideon said before God, “If you are going to save Israel through me, as you have said,

then look, I will lay this woolen fleece on the threshing floor [?]. If dew comes on the fleece alone and no water comes on all the ground, I will know that you will save Israel through me, as you have said.”
And it happened that way. Gideon rose early the next day and squeezed the wool. Dew water poured out of the woolen fleece, and he filled a bowl with water.

Gideon said to God, “Do not let your anger blaze against me. Let me speak this one more time. I will test you again with the fleece of wool. Let the fleece alone receive no water, but let dew fall on all the ground.”
God did this that night: no water came on the fleece alone, but dew came on all the ground.
Jerubbaal rose early in the morning, he and Gideon and all the people with him, and they camped by the spring of Harod. The camp of Midian was north of them, beyond the hill of Harod, in the valley.
The Lord said to Gideon, “The people with you are too numerous for me to hand Midian over to them. Otherwise Israel might boast against me, saying, ‘My own hand saved me.’
Now, then, speak in the hearing of the people.
[?] who lapped water with their mouths, I will save you and hand Midian over to you. Let all the people go, each to his own place.”

He took the people's provisions from them, along with their horn trumpets. Every man of Israel was sent away, each to his own tent, but he kept the three hundred men. The camp of Midian was below him in the valley.
That night the Lord said to him, “Get up and go down quickly from here to the camp, because I have handed it over to you.
But if you are afraid to go there, go to the camp with Purah your servant,

so that you may hear what they will say to you. After this, your hands will be strengthened, and you will go down to the camp.” He and Purah his servant went down to the first division of the enemy troops in the camp.
Midian, Amalek, and all the people of the east were lying in the valley, as numerous as locusts. Their camels were beyond counting, as numerous as the sand spread along the seashore.

Gideon came, and there was a man telling a dream to the man beside him. He said, “I had a dream: a cake of barley bread was rolling through the camp of Midian. It came to the camp and struck it, and the tent fell down.”
The man beside him said to him, “This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon son of Joash [?]”
[?] horn trumpets in their right hands to blow, and they shouted, saying, “The sword belongs to the Lord and to Gideon!”
Each man stood in his place around the camp. They blew the three hundred horn trumpets, and the whole camp fled. They cried out as they fled.
The Lord turned each man's sword against the man beside him throughout the camp. The whole camp fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the borders of Abel-meholah near Tabbath.
The men of Israel called out to Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh, and they pursued Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout the hill country of Ephraim, telling them, “Come out ahead of Midian and take control of the water as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.” All the men of Ephraim were called out, and they took control of the water as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.

They captured the two leaders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at Sur and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb, and they pursued Midian. They brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan.
The men of Ephraim said to him, “What is this you have done to us, not calling us too when you went to fight Midian?” They opposed him fiercely.
Gideon said to them, “What have I done now compared with what you have done? Aren't Ephraim's gleanings better than Abiezer's harvest?
God handed the rulers of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, over to you. And what was I able to do compared with what you yourselves did? Then their anger toward him cooled when he spoke these words to them.
Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed it, he and the three hundred men with him. They were hungry and were pursuing Midian.
He said to the men of Succoth, “Give some bread to these people following me so they can eat, because they are exhausted. I am pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.”
The leaders of Succoth said to him, “Are the heads of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your people?”
Gideon said to them, “For this reason, when the Lord hands Zebah and Zalmunna over to me, I will thresh your flesh with desert thorns and briers.” And
he went on from there up to Penuel and spoke to them in the same way. The men of Penuel answered him just as the men of Succoth had answered him.
Gideon said to the men of Penuel, “When I return in peace, I will tear down this tower.”

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army, about fifteen thousand men—all who remained of the entire army of the people of the east. Those who had fallen numbered one hundred and twenty thousand [?]
He said to Jether, his firstborn, “Get up and kill them.” But the boy did not draw his sword against them, because he was afraid, since he was still a young boy.

Zebah and Zalmunna said to Gideon, “Get up yourself and strike us, for your strength is like the strength of a mighty man.” Gideon got up and killed Zebah and Zalmunna. He took the crescent ornaments from their necks and from the necks of their camels.
The men of Israel spoke to Gideon, saying, “Sir, rule over us—you, your son, and your grandson—because you have rescued us from the power of Midian.”
Gideon said to them, “Neither I nor my son will rule over you. The Lord will rule over you.”
And Gideon said to them, “I ask one thing of you: let each of you give me a [?], an earring from your plunder.” For they had many gold earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.
They said to him, “We will gladly give them.” And Gideon spread out his garment, and each person threw a gold earring from his plunder onto it.

The weight of the gold earrings he had requested amounted to seventeen hundred gold pieces, apart from the crescent ornaments, the seals, and the purple garments that the king of Midian wore, and apart from the gold ornaments, which are [?], on the necks of their camels.
And Gideon [?]
[?] the olive tree said to them, “Should I leave behind my oil, through which people honor God, and go and be king over trees?”
And all the trees said to the fig tree, “Come and be queen over us.”
The fig tree said to them, “Should I leave behind my sweetness and my good fruit, and go and be queen over trees?”
And the trees said to the grapevine, “You come and be queen over us.”
The grapevine said to them, “Should I leave behind my wine, which makes people glad and through which they honor God and people, and go and stand over trees, ruling over them?”
And all the trees said to the bramble, “You come and be queen over us.”
The bramble said to the trees, “If you truly intend to appoint me queen over you, come and stand under my shade. Otherwise, let fire come out of me and consume the cedars of Lebanon.”

Now then, if you acted truthfully and with integrity when you made Abimelech king over you, and if you treated Jerubbaal and his household well, and if you treated him as the work of his hands deserved—
just as my father fought for you, risking his life in the face of our enemies, and rescued you from the power of Midian—

yet you rose up against my father’s household and killed his sons, seventy men, on a single stone, and made Abimelech, the son of his slave woman, king over the people of Shechem because he is your brother.
And if you have acted truthfully and with integrity toward Jerubbaal and his household today, may you rejoice in Abimelech, and may he also rejoice in you.

But if not, let fire come out of Abimelech and consume the people of Shechem and the household of Millo, and let fire come out of the people of Shechem and the household of Millo and consume Abimelech.
And Jonathan fled and went up to Beer. He stayed there, keeping away from his brother Abimelech.
And Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years.
And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the people of Shechem, and the people of Shechem rebelled against the house of Abimelech.
To bring the violence done to Jerubbaal’s seventy sons, and their blood, upon their brother Abimelech and upon the people of Shechem, because they had strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.
And the people of Shechem stationed men in ambush on the mountaintops. They robbed everyone traveling along the road when they encountered them, and Abimelech was informed.
Then Gaal son of Obel came with his brothers, and they passed through Shechem. And the people—[?]—and the people of Shechem put their trust in him.
And they went out into the fields, harvested their vineyards, trod the grapes, and made [?], that is, wine. They went into the house of their god, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech.

Gaal son of Obel said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is the son of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is this not the son of Jerubbaal? And is not Zebul, his servant, his overseer, together with the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem? Why should we serve him?”
“And who will put this people under my authority, so that I can remove Abimelech and say to him, ‘Increase your forces and come out!’”
Zebul, the ruler of the city, heard the words of Gaal son of Ebed and became furious.
He secretly sent messengers to Abimelech, saying, “Look, Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers are coming up to Shechem, and they will take up positions outside the city against you.
Now get up during the night, you and all the people with you, and lie in ambush in the countryside.
In the morning, when the sun rises, get an early start and come out toward the city. Look, he and the people with him will come out against you. Then do to him whatever you have the strength to do.”
Abimelech got up during the night, along with all the people with him, and they lay in ambush outside Shechem in four companies.
Early in the morning, Gaal son of Ebed came out and stood at the entrance to the city gate. Abimelech and the crowd with him rose from their hiding place.

When Gaal son of Ebed saw the crowd, he said to Zebul, “Look, people are coming down from the mountain peaks!” Zebul said to him, “You are seeing the shadows of the mountains as though they were people.”
Gaal spoke again, saying, “Look, a crowd is coming down from the west, beside the place near the center of the land. And look, another [?] crowd is coming along the road by the diviners’ tree.”
Zebul said to him, “Where is your mouth now, with which you said, ‘Who is Abimelech that we should serve him?’ Aren’t these the people you insulted? Go out now and fight them!”
Gaal went out ahead of the men of Shechem and took his stand to fight Abimelech.
Abimelech pursued him, and he fled from him. Many were wounded, all the way to the entrance of the gate.
Abimelech went into Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his brothers so that they could not live in Shechem.
The next day, the people went out into the countryside, and Abimelech was told.
He took his people, divided them into three companies, and lay in ambush in the countryside. He looked, and there were the people coming out of the city. He rose against them and struck them down.

Abimelech and the company with him—he sent them rushing out, and they took their stand at the entrance to the city gate. The other two companies rushed out against everyone in the countryside and struck them down.
Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the crowd within it. He demolished the city and turned it into salty ground.
When all the people of the tower of Shechem heard, they went up to the stronghold of the temple of Baal-berith.
Abimelech was told that all the men of the tower of Shechem had gathered together.

Abimelech went up Mount Hermon, along with the whole crowd that was with him. Abimelech took an axe in his hand, cut off a tree branch, picked it up, and put it on his shoulder. He said to the people with him, “What you have seen me do, do quickly yourselves, just as I did.”

Each person among all the people cut off a branch and picked it up. They followed Abimelech and placed the branches against the place where those people had gathered. He set the place on fire with them inside. All the people of the tower of Shechem died, about a thousand men and women.
Abimelech went up to the place called Thebez, camped against it, and captured it.

There was a large tower in the middle of the city. All the men of the city and the women fled there, along with everyone living in the city. They shut themselves in and went up onto the roof of the tower.
Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it. Then Abimelech advanced toward the entrance of the tower to burn it with fire.
A woman threw a piece of a millstone onto Abimelech’s head and crushed his skull.

He immediately called out to his servant who carried his weapons, saying to him, “Draw your sword and kill me, so that they do not say, ‘A woman killed him.’” His servant stabbed him with his sword, and he died there.
When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech had died, each went back to his own place.
God repaid Abimelech for the evil he had done to his father by killing his seventy brothers.
And God brought all the wickedness of the people of Shechem back on their own heads, and the curse of Jonathan son of Jerubbaal came upon them.
After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, the son of his father's brother, arose to save Israel. He was a man from Issachar, and he lived in Samaria in the hill country of Ephraim.
He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Samaria.
After him, Jair from Gilead arose, and he judged Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons who rode thirty donkeys. They had thirty towns, which are called the towns of Jair to this day. These are in Gilead.
Jair died, and they buried him in Ramnon.
The Israelites again did evil in the sight of the Lord. They served the Baals, the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, and the gods of Sidon [?]
The Israelites said to the Lord, "We have sinned. Do with us whatever seems good to you, but save us this day as well."
They removed the foreign gods from among them and served the Lord alone. And Israel grew discouraged in its suffering.
The Ammonites encamped in Gilead, and the Israelites also encamped at the lookout place, that is, the height. And
the leaders of the people of Gilead said to one another, "Who is the man who will undertake to fight the Ammonites? Let him become ruler over everyone who lives in Gilead."
Jephthah the Gileadite was mighty in strength. He was the son of a prostitute, who bore Jephthah to Gilead.
Gilead’s wife bore him sons. When his wife’s sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out, saying to him, “You will not inherit anything in our father’s house, because you are the son of a prostitute.”
Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land called Tob. Worthless men gathered around Jephthah and went out with him.
After some time, the Ammonites went to war against Israel.
The elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.
They said to Jephthah, "Come and be our leader, so that we may fight the Ammonites."
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “Was it not you who hated me and drove me out from among you and out of my father’s house? Why have you come to me now, since you are in distress?”
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have now come to you. Come with us, fight the Ammonites, and become ruler over everyone who lives in Gilead."
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me to fight the Ammonites, and the Lord hands them over to me, I will become your ruler."
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "May the Lord hear this agreement between all of us if we do not act according to it."
Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people appointed him as their leader and head. Jephthah spoke all his words before the Lord at Mizpah.
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, saying to him, "What quarrel do you have with me, that you have come against me to fight in my land?"

The king of the Ammonites said to Jephthah's messengers, "Because Israel took my land when it came out of Egypt, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and as far as the Jordan. Now return these lands to me peacefully." And the messengers returned to Jephthah.
Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites,
Saying to him, “This is what Jephthah says: Israel took the land of Moab and the land of the Ammonites,
when they came up from Egypt. But when Israel traveled through the wilderness as far as the Red Sea and as far as Kadesh,

And Israel sent messengers to the king of the Edomites, saying to him, “I want to pass through your land.” But the king of Edom would not listen. He also sent messengers to the king of Moab, but he too refused. So Israel stayed in Kadesh.

Israel traveled through the wilderness, went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab, and came from the east into the land of Moab. They encamped on the other side of the Arnon and did not enter Moab's territory, because the Arnon is Moab's boundary.
And Israel sent messengers to Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon. Israel said to him, “Let me pass through your land to my own place.”
But Sihon did not trust Israel enough to let them pass through his territory. Sihon gathered all his people, and they stationed themselves at Jahaz and fought against Israel.
And the Lord, the God of Israel, handed Sihon and all his people over to Israel, who defeated him. And Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites,
from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
Now the Lord, the God of Israel, is the one who removed the Amorites before his people Israel, and are you going to take possession of their land?
Is it not what Chemosh your god has given you to possess that you will possess? Likewise, all the others whom the Lord our God destroyed before us are those whose land we will possess.
Now then, are you really better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend with Israel or wage war against them?

While Israel lived in Heshbon and its surrounding territory, in the land of Aroer and its surrounding territory, and in all the other cities beside the Jordan for three hundred and thirty years, why did you not recover them during that time?
I have not wronged you, but you are going to do me harm by fighting against me. Let God judge between the Israelites and the Ammonites.
But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words Jephthah sent him.
And the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh, and he passed through the lookout post of Gilead toward the territory of the Ammonites.
And Jephthah made a vow to the Lord, saying, “If you will indeed hand the Ammonites over to me,
then whoever first comes out through the door of my house to meet me when I return safely from the Ammonites, I will offer that one up to the Lord.”
And Jephthah went to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the Lord handed them over to him.
He struck them down from Aroer as far as Arnon, twenty-five cities in all, and as far as the vineyards, inflicting a very great defeat. And the Ammonites were humbled before the Israelites.

And Jephthah came home to Mizpah, and there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. She was his only daughter, whom he loved; he had no other son or daughter besides her.

When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said to her, “Oh, my daughter! You have terribly distressed me, and you are part of my distress. I have opened my mouth to the Lord concerning you, and I cannot turn back.”

And the young woman said to [?], “My father, if you have opened your mouth to the Lord concerning me, do to me what came out of your mouth, since the Lord has taken vengeance on your enemies, the Ammonites.”
She also said to her father, “Let my father do this for me: leave me alone for two months, so that I may go away into the mountains and mourn my virginity, together with my friends.”
He said to her, “Go.” And he sent her away for two months. She went with her friends, and they mourned her virginity in the mountains.

At the end of the two months, she returned to her father, and he did to her according to the vow he had made. She had never had sexual relations with a man. And this became an established practice in Israel:
year after year, the daughters of Israel went to mourn the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite for four days each year.
And the men of Ephraim gathered and came up to Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, “Why did you go to fight against the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We will burn your house down over you.”
And they said to Jephthah, “I am a warrior, along with my people, and the Ammonites oppressed me severely. I called out to you, but you did not rescue me from their hands.”
I saw that I had not been rescued, so I took my life in my hands and went against the Ammonites, and the Lord handed them over to me. Why, then, have you come against me today to fight me?

Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead, and they fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck down Ephraim because those who had escaped from Ephraim had said, “You Gileadites are in the midst of Ephraim and in the midst of Manasseh.”

The men of Gilead seized the crossing places of the Jordan belonging to Ephraim. Those who had escaped from Ephraim said, “Let us cross.” The men of Gilead asked them, “Are you from Ephraim?” They said, “No.”

They said to them, “Say ‘Quickly.’” And they could not pronounce it correctly. They seized them and killed them at the crossing places of the Jordan. At that time, forty-two thousand from Ephraim fell.
Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died, and they buried him in his city, Gilead.
After him, Ibzan from Bethlehem judged Israel.
He had thirty sons and thirty daughters whom he sent away, and he brought in thirty other daughters from outside for his sons. He judged Israel for seven years.
Then Ibzan died, and they buried him in Bethlehem.
After him, Elon the Zebulunite arose and judged Israel for ten years.
Elon the Zebulunite died, and they buried him in Aijalon, in the land of Zebulun.
After him, Abdon son of Sellem, the Pirathonite, judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty daughters of his sons, who rode on seventy donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years.
Abdon son of Sellem, the Pirathonite, died, and they buried him in Pirathon, in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of Lanak.
The Israelites again did evil in the Lord’s sight, and the Lord handed them over to the Philistines for forty years.
There was a man from Zorah, from the tribe of Dan, whose name was Manoah. His wife was barren and had not given birth.
And an angel of the Lord appeared to his wife and said to her, “Look, you are barren and have not given birth, but you will conceive and bear a son.”
Now be careful not to drink wine or strong drink, and not to eat anything unclean.

For look, you are pregnant and will give birth to a son. No razor must touch his head, because the child will be a Nazirite of God from his birth. He will begin to save Israel from the hands of the Philistines.

The woman went in and told her husband, “A man of God came to me. His appearance was like that of an angel of God, very frightening. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name.

He said to me, ‘Look, you are pregnant and will give birth to a son. Now, then, do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean, because the child will be a Nazirite of God from the day of his birth until the day of his death.’”
Manoah prayed to the Lord, saying, “Hear me, Lord Adonai. Let the man of God whom you sent come again and teach us what we should do for the child who will be born.”
God listened to Manoah’s voice, and the angel of God came again to his wife while she was sitting in the field. Manoah, her husband, was not with her.
The woman immediately ran and told her husband, “Look, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me.”
Manoah, her husband, got up and followed his wife. He came to the man and said to him, “Are you the man who spoke with the woman?” The angel said, “I am.”
Manoah said to him, “Now, when your word comes true, what rule will apply to the child, and what will his work be?”
The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “Let her observe everything I told your wife.
She must not eat anything that comes from the grapevine, drink wine or strong drink, or eat anything unclean. She must observe everything I commanded her.”
Manoah said to the angel of the Lord, “Let her be careful, Lord. But we will keep you here and prepare a young goat before you.”

The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “Even if you keep me here, I will not eat your bread. If you prepare a burnt offering, you must offer it to the Lord.” For Manoah did not know that he was an angel of the Lord.
Manoah said to the angel, “What is your name, so that when your words come true, we may honor you?”
And the angel of the Lord said to him, “Why are you asking about my name? It is wonderful.”
Manoah took the young goat and the offering and brought them up onto the rock for the Lord. And he [?] to do it, while Manoah and his wife watched him.

When the flame of the fire rose from the altar toward heaven, the angel of the Lord went up to heaven in the flame of the altar. Manoah and his wife were watching him, and they fell facedown on the ground.
The angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah and his wife. Then Manoah realized that he was an angel of the Lord.
Manoah said to his wife, “We will certainly die, because we have seen God.”

His wife said to him, “If the Lord had wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted the burnt offering and the offering from our hands. He would not have shown us all these things, nor would he have let us hear these things at their appointed time.”
The woman gave birth to the son and named him Samson. The little boy grew, and the Lord blessed him.
And the Spirit of the Lord began to go out with him in the camp of Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah and saw a woman there among the daughters of the Philistines. She pleased him.
He went up and told his father and mother, saying to them, “I saw a woman in Timnah among the daughters of the Philistines. Now get her for me as my wife.”

His father and mother said to him, “Is there no daughter among your relatives or among all our people who could become your wife, that you must go and get yourself a wife from these uncircumcised Philistines?” Samson said to his father, “Get this woman for me, because she is the one who pleases me.”
His father and mother did not know that this decision came from the Lord, for he was seeking revenge on the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
Samson went down with his father and mother. They went down to Timnah and came to the vineyards of Timnah. Suddenly a young lion came toward him, roaring.

And the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him. He tore the young lion apart as someone would kill a young goat, though he had nothing in his hand. But he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.
They went down and spoke with the woman, and the matter seemed right to Samson.
After some days he returned to take her, and he turned aside to look at the carcass, or body, of the lion. There was a swarm of bees in the lion’s mouth, along with honey.

He scooped the honey into his hands and walked along eating it. He came to his father and mother and gave them some, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the lion’s mouth.
His father came to the woman, and Samson held a feast there for seven days, because that is what young men customarily did.
When they saw him, they brought thirty young men to be with him.

Samson said to them, “I will tell you a riddle. If you can fully explain it to me during the seven days of the feast and find its answer, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothing.
But if you cannot explain it to me, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothing.” They said to him, “Tell us your riddle so that we can hear it.”
He said to them, “Something to eat came out of the eater, and something sweet came out of the strong.” They could not explain the riddle by the third day.
On the fourth day they said to Samson’s wife, “Persuade your husband to tell you his riddle, or we will burn you and your father’s house with fire. Or did you invite us to make us poor?”

Samson’s wife wept before him, saying to him, “Why do you hate me like this and not love me? Why have you not told me the riddle you told the people of my nation?” Samson said to her, “If I have not told it to my father and mother, should I tell it to you?”
She kept weeping before him during the seven days of the feast. On the seventh day he told her, because she kept bothering him. She in turn told it to the people of her nation.

The men of the city said to him on the seventh day, before the sun set, “What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?” Samson said to them, “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have understood my riddle.”

And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him. He got up and went down to Ashkelon, killed thirty of their men, took their clothes, and gave their garments to those who had answered the riddle. Samson was furious, and he got up and went up to his father’s house.
Samson’s wife lived with one of his friends, those who had accompanied him.
After some days, during the wheat harvest, Samson visited his wife with a young goat, saying, “I will go in to my wife in her room.” But her father would not let him go in to her.
Her father said to him, “I thought you utterly hated her, so I gave her to one of your friends. Isn’t her younger sister better than she is? Take her instead.”
Samson said to them, “Now I will bear no guilt toward the Philistines when I do them harm.”
He caught three hundred foxes and took torches. He tied one tail to another and placed a torch between each pair of tails, fastening it to them.
He lit a fire in the torches and sent them into the Philistines’ grain fields. They burned everything from the heaps of sheaves to the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive trees.

The Philistines said to one another, “Who has done this to us?” They said, “It was Samson, who married the Timnite’s daughter, because her father took his wife and gave her to one of his friends.” The Philistines went up and burned her and her father with fire.
Samson said to them, “If you do things like this, it is not what I want. But I will take my revenge on each one of you, and afterward I will stop.”
He struck them, hitting their shins against their thighs, in a very great slaughter. Samson went down and stayed beside the rock of Etam.
The Philistines came up and went to fight against Judah. They stayed at the place called Lehi.
The men of Judah said to them, “Why have you come up to fight against us?” The Philistines said to them, “We have come up to bind Samson and do to him what he did to us.”

Three thousand men from Judah went down to the cleft in the rock of Etam. They said to Samson, “Don’t you know that the Philistines rule over us? What is this you have done to us?” Samson said to them, “As they did to me, so I did to them.”
They said to him, “We have come down to bind you and hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson said to them, “Swear to me that you yourselves will not kill me, but will hand me over to them.”

They swore to him, saying, “We will not kill you, but will tie you up and hand you over to them. We certainly will not put you to death.” They tied him with two new ropes and brought him up from that rock.

He came down to the place called Jawbone, and the Philistines shouted and ran toward him. But the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and the ropes bound around his arms became like flax set ablaze with fire. The ropes came loose from his arms.
He found a donkey’s jawbone lying on the ground. He reached out his hand, picked it up, and killed a thousand men with it.
Samson said, “With a donkey’s jawbone, I swept away the Philistines in one sweep. With the donkey’s jawbone, I struck down a thousand men.”
When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone out of his hand. He called that place “The Lifting Up,” or “The Raising of the Jawbone.”

He was very thirsty and cried out to the Lord, saying, “You are the one who has granted this great deliverance through the hand of your servant. And now am I to die of thirst and fall into the hands of these uncircumcised men?”

And God opened the hollow at the place of the Jawbone, and water came out of it. He drank, his spirit recovered, and he revived. For this reason he named it “The Spring of the One Who Calls.” It remains at that place, the place of the Jawbone, to this day.
He judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
Samson went down to Gaza. There he saw a prostitute and went in to her.

The people of Gaza were told, “Samson has come here.” They surrounded the house and lay in wait for him all night at the city gate. They remained silent all night, saying, “When the morning light comes, let us get up and kill him.”

Samson slept until midnight. At midnight he got up, took hold of the doors of the city gate and its two posts, and pulled them up along with their bar. He put them on his shoulders, carried them to the top of the mountain facing Hebron, and left [?] there.
After this, he fell in love with a woman in the valley of Sorek whose name was Delilah.

The rulers of the Philistines went up to her and said, “Deceive him and find out where his great strength lies and how we can overpower him and bind him so that we can subdue him. We will give you a thousand [?] and a hundred pieces of silver.”
Delilah said to Samson, “Tell me where your great strength lies and what you could be bound with so that you could be subdued.”
Samson said to her, “If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become weak and be like any other man.”
The rulers of the Philistines brought her the seven bowstrings that had not yet been dried, and she tied him with them.

The ambush party was waiting in the inner room. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” And he snapped the cords as someone would snap a flax thread when fire touches it. And they did not discover the source of his strength.
Delilah said to Samson, “Look, you have deceived me and lied to me. Now tell me what you could be bound with.”
He said to her, “If they tie me securely with seven new ropes that have never been used for any work, I will become weak and be like any other man.”

Delilah took the new ropes and tied him with them. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” The men lying in wait were sitting in the inner room. But he tore the ropes off his arms like a thread.

Delilah said to Samson, “Look, you have deceived me again and spoken lies to me. Now tell me what you could be bound with.” He said to her, “If you take and weave the seven locks of hair on my head into the warp, and fasten them with the peg into the loom, I will become weak and be like any other man.”

When he lay down to sleep, Delilah took the seven locks of hair on his head, wove them into the warp, and fastened them with the peg into the loom. She said, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He awoke from his sleep and pulled the peg out of the loom with the warp attached to it. They did not discover the source of his strength.
Delilah said to Samson, “How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not open to me? This is the third time you have deceived me, and you have not told me where your great strength lies.”
When she pressed him all night with her words and tormented him, he became weary to the point of death.

He revealed everything in his heart to her, saying, “No razor has ever touched my head, because I have been a Nazirite dedicated to God since I was in my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I too will become weak and be like any other man.”

Delilah realized that he had revealed everything in his heart to her. She sent for the rulers of the Philistines, saying to them, “Come up to me this once more, because he has revealed everything in his heart to me.” And they came.
“Look, the Philistines have come against you!” Samson roused himself, saying, “I will get up and fall upon them.” [?] His strength had left him.
The Philistines rushed at him, gouged out his eyes, brought him down to Gaza, and bound him.

He gave eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother. His mother said, “I have solemnly dedicated the silver from my hand to the Lord, to make a carved image and a cast image for my son. And now I will give it to you.”
He gave the silver to his mother, and his mother took two hundred pieces of silver [?] and gave them to the silversmith. He made a cast image and a carved image, and [?] in Micah’s house.
The man Micah had a priest of God. He made an ephod and teraphim, and he ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.
In those days there was no king in Israel. Each person did what was right in his own eyes.
There was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah. He was a Levite living there.
The man left Bethlehem, the city in Judah, to stay wherever he could find a place. He came to the hill country of Ephraim, to lodge at Micah’s house as he continued his journey.
Micah said to him, “Where are you coming from?” He said to him, “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am traveling to stay wherever I can find a place.”
Micah said to him, “Stay with me and be a father and a priest to me. I will give you ten pieces of silver daily, a set of clothes, and what you need to live on.”
The Levite went and decided to stay with the man. The young man remained with him like one of his sons.
Micah consecrated the Levite, and the young man became a priest and remained in Micah’s house.
Micah said, “Now I know that the Lord will do good to me, because a Levite has become my priest.”

In those days there was no king in Israel. In those days the tribe of Dan was looking for an inheritance to live in, because until that day no inheritance had become theirs among the tribes of Israel.

The people of Dan sent five men from their clans, capable men from their territory, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to explore the land and investigate it. They said to them, “Go and explore the land.” They came to the hill country of Ephraim, to Micah’s house, and lodged there. While they were staying
in the house with Micah, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. They said to him, “Who brought you here? What are you doing here? And what do you have here?”
He said to them, “This is what Micah did for me: he hired me, and I became his priest.”
They said to him, “Please ask God for us, so that we may know whether the journey we are going on will succeed.”
The priest said to them, “Go in peace. The journey you are going on is right before the Lord.”
The five men traveled on and came down to Laish. They saw the people within it [?].

They turned around and said to Micah, “What has happened to you that you are crying out?”
Micah said to them, “Because you have taken my gods, which I made for myself, and the priest, and you have gone away! What do I have left now? And you say to me, ‘Why are you shouting?’”
The Danites said to him, “Now do not let your voice be heard among us, or some men among us who are angry may attack you and destroy your life and the lives of your household.”
The Danites went on their way. When Micah saw that they were stronger than he was, he returned to his house.

The Danites took what Micah had made and the priest who served him. They came to Laish, to a people who were quiet and living securely and confidently. They struck them down with the edge of the sword, and he burned the city with fire.

There was no one to rescue it, because it was far from the people of Sidon and because they had no dealings with the people of Syria. The city was in the valley of Beth-rehob. They rebuilt the city and settled in it.
They named the city Dan, after their ancestor Dan, who was born to Israel. The city had formerly been called Ulamais.

The Danites set up Micah’s carved image for themselves. Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, and his sons served as priests for the tribe of Dan until the day the land went into captivity.
They kept the carved image that Micah had made for himself throughout all the days when the house of God was in Shiloh. In those days there was no king in Israel.
There was a Levite living in the outlying parts of the hill country of Ephraim. He took a woman from Bethlehem in Judah as his concubine.
But his concubine withdrew from him and went to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah. She stayed there for four months.

Her husband got up and went to speak tenderly to her and bring her back to his house. He had a young servant with him and two donkeys. He came to her father’s house, and she brought him inside her father’s house. When the young woman’s father saw him, he got up and welcomed him joyfully.
His father-in-law, the young woman’s father, stayed with him for three days. They ate and drank and stayed in that place.
On the fourth day they rose early in the morning and got up to leave. The young woman’s father said to his daughter’s husband, “Strengthen yourself with a little bread, and afterward you can go.”
He sat down, and the two of them ate and drank together. The young woman’s father said to her husband, “Stay here today as well, and enjoy yourself.”
The man got up to leave, but his father-in-law pressed him, and he stayed again for [?].

[?] an old man who had come back from his field after finishing his work in the evening. The old man was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living as a foreigner in Gibeah. The people of that place were sons of Belial.
He looked up and saw the traveler in the city square. The old man said to him, “Where are you going, and where have you come from?”

He said to him, “We have come from Bethlehem in Judah and are going to the outlying parts of the hill country of Ephraim. I am from there. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going home. But no one has taken me into his house.
There is straw and fodder for the animals, and there is bread and wine for me, your female servant, and the young man. Your servants lack nothing.”
The old man said to him, “Peace be with you. I will take care of everything you need. I will not let you stay in the square.”
He brought them into his house, cared for the animals, and put fodder before them. He also washed his guests’ feet, and they ate and drank.

While they were enjoying themselves, the men of the city, who were lawless men, surrounded the house and beat on the door. They said to the old man who owned the house, “Bring out the man who came into your house, so that we can have sex with him.”
The man who owned the house went out and said to them, “No, my brothers! Do not do evil to this man. Since he has entered my house, do not commit this outrage.”
“Here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. I will bring them out to you, and you can do to them whatever seems good to you. But do not do this outrageous thing to this man.”

But the men would not listen to him. So the man seized his concubine and brought her outside to them. They had sex with her, and they had sex with her all night until morning. They let her go when daylight came.
The woman came early in the morning to where the man was and collapsed at the door of the house where her master was. She remained there until daylight spread.
Her master opened the doors of the house and went out to continue on his way. There was his concubine, lying at the door of the house with her hands on the threshold.
He said to her, “Get up. Let us go.” But she gave him no answer, for she was dead. He lifted her onto his donkey and set off for his own place. Then he entered his house.
He took the knife, seized his concubine, and cut her apart, limb by limb, along her bones, into twelve pieces. He sent them out to all the tribes of Israel.

And everyone who saw them said, “Nothing like this has happened, and nothing like this has been seen, from the days when the Israelites came up out of Egypt until this day.” And he instructed the men whom he sent, saying, “This is what you are to say before all the people of Israel: ‘Has anything like this happened from the day when the Israelites came up out of the land of Egypt until today? Consider this matter, take counsel about it, and speak.’”
And all the Israelites came out, and the whole assembly gathered together as one person, from Dan to Beersheba, along with the land of Gilead, before the Lord at Mizpah.
And all the tribes of Israel stood before the Lord in the assembly of God's people. There were four hundred thousand men on foot, armed with swords.
And the Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had come up to Mizpah. And the Israelites said, “Where did this wickedness happen?”
And the man who was a Levite, the husband of the woman who had been killed, answered them, saying, “I came up to Gibeah, the city of Benjamin, with my concubine, to spend the night there.
And the men of Gibeah rose up against me and surrounded me in the house at night. They wanted to kill me, and they violated my concubine and mocked her, and she died.
I took hold of my concubine, cut her up limb by limb, and sent her throughout all the territories of Israel's inheritance, because they had committed an outrage in Israel.
Look, all of you Israelites are here. Give your judgment and counsel so that it may reach that place.”
And all the people rose as one person, saying, “None of us will go to his dwelling, and no one will return to his house.
Now this is what will happen to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot.

But we will appoint ten men out of every hundred from the tribes of Israel, a hundred out of every thousand, and a thousand out of every ten thousand, to get provisions for the people, so that they may go up to Gibeah, the city of Benjamin, to deal with them according to all the outrage they committed in Israel.”
And all the men of Israel gathered against the city as one person.
And the tribes of Israel sent men throughout the whole tribe of Benjamin, saying to them, “What is this wickedness that has happened among you?

Now hand over to us the ungodly men, the sons of Belial who are in Gibeah, so that we may kill them and remove the wickedness from Israel.” But the Benjaminites were unwilling to listen to their brothers, the Israelites.
And the Benjaminites gathered from their cities at Gibeah to go out and fight against their brothers, the Israelites.
And that day the Benjaminites from their cities were counted: twenty thousand five hundred men armed with swords. [?]
